name: Individual false lashes / magnetic lashes

image.caption: Vintage false lashes and hat box

lead: False lashes add length and density to the lash line the moment they go on. Individual lashes are applied one by one by a technician, while magnetic lashes clamp on with small magnets and come off daily.

The synthetic lashes attach to or clamp around natural lashes, adding visible length and volume without changing the natural lash. Individual extensions last a few weeks. Artificial lashes date back more than a century, and magnetic versions were invented in 2014 as a glue-free option. No clinical studies were found.

paras: Individual lashes are booked with a technician and refilled periodically; magnetic lashes are put on at home for an occasion or daily and removed at night. Both are often paired with mascara or eyeliner.
Adhesives used for glued lashes can cause skin sensitivity in some people, and magnetic lashes may pose a hazard near MRI machines.

web.title: Eyelid Cosmetic Enhancements and Their Associated Ocular Adverse Effects

chain: Artificial lashes attach to lash line
angle.text: Users add strip, individual or magnetic lashes for instant length and volume. The artificial lashes attach to the lash line, so the fuller look is visible right away and temporary. No clinical research on the products was found.

lead: False eyelashes are artificial lashes attached to or near the natural lash line to add length, volume and density. Individual lash extensions are applied one at a time by a technician; magnetic lashes clamp onto the natural lashes without glue; strip lashes are glued on temporarily. People use them for an instantly fuller, darker lash line that makes the eyes look larger, more defined and more open [1].

Extensions are customised to the client's eye shape and natural lashes in material, length, colour and curl, with styles ranging from a natural classic set to a hybrid and a full volume set. Application can take up to two hours and a set typically lasts three to four weeks [1]. Magnetic lashes are reusable and need no adhesive [1].

Artificial lashes date back more than a century, and magnetic lashes were invented in 2014 by Katy Stoka [1]. Published research is mainly on adverse effects: a 2019 review of case reports found allergic blepharitis the most common complication linked to extensions [2]. No clinical study has tested the cosmetic effect itself.
infobox: Up to two hours for extensions [1]

paras: Strip lashes are synthetic, trimmable strips fixed above the natural lashes with temporary glue and removed with warm water or eye makeup remover; they are not meant to be worn while showering, sleeping or swimming [1]. Individual extensions are attached one by one to natural lashes with semi-permanent adhesive, usually by a technician, using synthetic or natural lashes [1]. Magnetic lashes use a thin magnetic strip attached to the false lash that sandwiches the natural lashes, so no adhesive is needed, and they are reusable and affordable [1].

A report from 1882 described Parisians sewing hair into the eyelids, and a 1899 newspaper account described a similar method as painful. Karl Nessler patented artificial lashes in the UK in 1902-1903, Anna Taylor patented a fabric-strip design in the US in 1911, and false lashes became popular in the early 1930s and again in the 1960s [1]. Magnetic lashes followed in 2014 [1].

A 2019 review of eyelid cosmetic enhancements covered 53 eyelash extension cases drawn from 18 case reports: 42 allergic blepharitis, 4 keratoconjunctivitis, 3 conjunctival erosion, 2 contact dermatitis, 1 bacterial keratitis and 1 subconjunctival erosion. The authors link the allergic cases to allergens in acrylate adhesives, which can release formaldehyde, and note that bacteria can collect under the lash bed when hygiene is limited [2].

Wikipedia notes that magnetic lashes may pose a hazard in MRI scanning rooms because of their magnets, and recounts that an actress's eyes swelled nearly shut after lashes were glued on for a 1916 film [1]. A general review of contact dermatitis to cosmetics covers allergic reactions to cosmetic ingredients, though it does not address lashes specifically.

No studies found of the cosmetic effect of individual or magnetic lashes. Safety information comes from case reports collected in a 2019 review of eyelid cosmetic enhancements [2]. Related laboratory work on lash cosmetics includes a 2020 formulation study of a curling mascara using a thermoresponsive polymer, which is not a study of false lashes [3].
